title: Account A to B Transfer

questions.question: One database transaction
questions.answer:
Validate source != destination, positive amount, same currency and authorization. Persist a transfer request with a unique business reference. Lock the request, then both account rows in ascending account ID order. Check both accounts are active and source funds are sufficient. Debit source, credit destination, record linked debit/credit ledger entries, mark the request successful and commit together.

Use DECIMAL or integer minor units for money, never binary floating-point arithmetic. The two ledger amounts must balance. Balance is current state; the ledger preserves history.

questions.question: Deadlocks and external boundaries
questions.answer:
Deterministic lock order reduces deadlocks but does not eliminate all deadlocks. Retry a rolled-back database-only operation with the same idempotency key and bounded attempts. Do not include a bank HTTP call inside a transaction closure that may be retried.

An external bank transfer is not atomic with your local database. Use a durable payment intent/outbox, bank reference, idempotent adapter, callbacks and reconciliation.

summary: Move ₹5,000 from account A to B while another request moves ₹2,000 from B to A. Follow deterministic locks and balanced ledger entries.
example_label: Illustrative production scenario — fictional educational records

paragraphs: Account A (101) starts with ₹10,000 and B (202) starts with ₹3,000, both INR and ACTIVE. Transfer 8001 moves ₹5,000 A → B; a separate concurrent transfer 8002 moves ₹2,000 B → A. Both are authorized positive-amount internal transfers.

The combined balance must remain ₹13,000. In the illustrated order, the first transfer yields A=₹5,000/B=₹8,000; the second yields A=₹7,000/B=₹6,000. A partial debit without its matching credit must never commit.
This lesson is a transfer within one database and currency. Transfers to an external bank need the separate adapter/reconciliation workflow; database atomicity does not cross that boundary.

paragraphs: The transfer controller verifies the customer controls the source and the destination is a valid recipient. The service locks transfer_requests.id=8001 and returns the saved outcome on repeated delivery.

Read source/destination IDs from the saved request, sort their numeric IDs, and lock them with two point reads in that order. Both directions therefore lock 101 before 202. Check statuses, currency and funds after locks are acquired.

Guard the source debit, credit the destination, insert both uniquely referenced ledger entries, set request SUCCESS and append audit/outbox rows. Any error rolls back every local effect. Send no external HTTP call while these account locks are held.

paragraphs: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is a locking read inside an explicit InnoDB transaction. The row remains protected until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Use indexed primary/unique lookups so the operation does not scan and lock unrelated data.

Every handler touching multiple entities must follow the same lock hierarchy. Define it once for workers, callbacks and reconcilers; opposite order can create deadlocks. A deadlock victim must restart the whole local transaction and re-read data.
Lock transfer request first, then account 101 and 202 in ascending order for both directions. READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ does not fix an application that performs unlocked balance decisions.

If the destination credit or either ledger insert fails, rollback the source debit as well. Inactive account, currency mismatch, same-account transfer and insufficient funds are distinct validation/business failures. Never record a debit-only SUCCESS.

Use TR-CLIENT-001 again for a retry of transfer 8001. A bounded deadlock retry restarts the entire local transaction, re-reads locked balances and inserts no duplicate ledger entries. The original request ID and unique ledger pair prevent repeated effects.

items: Why lock 101 before 202 for both directions?
A consistent lock order avoids the classic cycle where each worker holds one account while waiting for the other.
Can one ledger insert be committed if the other fails?
No. Debit, credit, both ledger entries and request result form one local transaction.
Why SELECT FOR UPDATE?
Protect a mutable row while the transaction makes and applies a decision from its current value.
What does a waiting request read?
The new committed value after obtaining its lock, not a cached value from before waiting.
Why cannot local rollback reverse a bank payment?
The bank is outside the local transaction boundary; use verified reconciliation and a separate authorized reversal/refund.
How are duplicate webhooks prevented from repeating money effects?
Authenticate the event, persist unique provider/business keys, lock the saved payment and apply the final result once.
What distinguishes FAILED, PENDING and UNKNOWN?
Confirmed rejection; confirmed work in progress; and unresolved external outcome, respectively.
How do 5,000 student payments or 10,000 salaries scale?
Persist independent obligations, use controlled idempotent workers, avoid long global locks, and reconcile each result.
Why queue receipt generation?
Document availability can retry independently without changing a confirmed financial outcome.
What should a deadlock retry repeat?
The entire rolled-back local transaction with its original business identity; never an uncertain external payment.
